description_full: Vail Resorts, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates mountain resorts and regional ski areas in the United States and internationally. The company operates in three segments: Mountain, Lodging, and Real Estate. The Mountain segment operates destination mountain resorts and regional ski areas. This segment is also involved in ancillary activities, including ski school, dining, and retail/rental operations, as well as real estate brokerage activities. The lodging segment owns and manages various luxury hotels and condominiums under the RockResorts brand; operates other lodging properties and various condominiums; and offers resort ground transportation services. The Real Estate segment owns, develops, and sells real estate properties. Vail Resorts, Inc. was founded in 1962 and is based in Broomfield, Colorado.

CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Vail Resorts, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $5.5B market cap on $2.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 7% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $248M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.25× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.0× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 6.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.5) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Very elevated short interest (25.9% of float) — sophisticated money is betting against the business
Payout ratio looks stretched — the dividend’s own margin of safety is thin
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 12% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Shares offer a 19% margin of safety against estimated fair value
Large open-market insider purchases (net $5.0M) — management putting its own capital behind the business
14 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 7pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.87x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+13.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.28 vs 5y 0.81), so read it loosely.
About $94.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 36% in the 2022 bear market and 72% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 19% below its DCF fair value of $188, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $129 to $275 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 37.0 vs 18.8 and P/FCF 22.0 vs 16.7 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-9%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $148 on average, 3% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 7.4%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.42).
It converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.25x.
ROE of 61% is amplified by 23.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.0x net debt to EBITDA ($268.5M of cash against $3.2B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.51 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.80 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.6% over 3 years, 8.2% over 5 years and 5.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 11.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -9.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (8.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.4%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (2 purchases, net $5.0M bought).
It returns 6.6% a year to shareholders (0.8% in buybacks and 5.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 216% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 25.9% of the float, 9.4 days to cover.
people: With about 6,500 employees, each generates about $437K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 6.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $38K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.3M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
